name: gender of nouns
title: Spanish Noun Gender Practice: Masculine or Feminine Quiz
description: Practice the gender of Spanish nouns: -o and -a endings, -ción, -dad and -ma words, exceptions like el día and la mano, and people, with 10 checked sentences.
answer: Every Spanish noun is masculine or feminine. Most nouns ending in -o are masculine and most ending in -a are feminine, while -ción, -sión, -dad, -tad and -tud are feminine. Many Greek words in -ma are masculine (el problema, el idioma), and a few frequent nouns break the pattern: el día, el mapa, la mano, la foto, la moto.

rules.example: el libro, el carro, el vaso
la casa, la mesa, la ventana
la canción, la ciudad, la libertad, la juventud

quiz.after: canción de la película es muy famosa.

quiz.why: Problema keeps -a and is masculine: un problema.
Día is masculine (un día) and takes an accent.
Mano is a feminine exception: la mano.

quiz.after: ciudad de Nueva York es enorme.

quiz.why: Estudiante has one form; the article shows the person: una estudiante.
Foto is short for fotografía, feminine: la foto.

quiz.after: amistad es muy importante para mí.

quiz.why: Mapa is a masculine exception: el mapa.

mistakes: Changing -a words to -o: «el problemo» should be «el problema».
Assuming every -a word is feminine: el día, el mapa, el planeta, el idioma and el sistema are masculine.
Using el with -ción and -dad words: «el canción» should be «la canción».
Thinking gender is about meaning: a table is not «female»; gender is a grammar category you learn with each noun.
Forgetting that shortened words keep the original gender: la foto (fotografía), la moto (motocicleta), la tele (televisión).

heritage: Heritage speakers usually know the gender of everyday nouns. Variation appears with English loanwords used in the US: el or la app, el or la email, el or la parking. Dictionaries list el correo electrónico and la aplicación; for loanwords, follow the most common form in your community and stay consistent.
teacher: Make two piles, masculine and feminine, with noun cards. Students sort them and then explain the hard ones (el día, la mano) to their group. Finish with a quick article race.

faq.question: Do Spanish nouns really have gender?
faq.answer: Yes. Every noun is grammatically masculine or feminine, and articles and adjectives agree with it: el carro rojo, la casa roja. It is a grammar feature, not a statement about the object.

faq.question: What are the best rules for guessing gender?
faq.answer: Nouns in -o are usually masculine and in -a usually feminine. Words in -ción, -sión, -dad, -tad and -tud are feminine. Many words in -ma are masculine. Always learn new nouns with their article.

faq.question: What about nouns ending in -e or a consonant?
faq.answer: They can be either: el coche, la noche; el papel, la miel. There is no reliable rule, so learn the article with the word: el árbol, la flor.
